title: The Build That Rebuilt Nothing or Everything: Timestamps, Content and a Cache That Never Serves Stale Output

questions.question: A source file is restored from a backup and has an older timestamp than the object built from the file it replaced. What does a timestamp-based build do?
options: Says it is up to date and uses the old object
questions.explanation: The source is not newer than the output. The text had changed and the timestamp was 400 against an object at 1000.

questions.question: A file is built, edited and reverted. How many compiles by timestamp and by content?
options: 3 and 2: the revert finds the object of the first build
questions.explanation: After a touch the timestamp said rebuild and the content key hit.

questions.question: What does the build key contain, and why?
options: The name, the text and the flags
questions.explanation: An output depends on all three. The same source with -O0 and -O2 are different builds.

questions.question: Why are the three names multiplied by large constants before xor?
options: So that two equal parts do not cancel to zero and swapping two fields does not give the same key
questions.explanation: build_key(x, y, z) differs from build_key(y, x, z).

questions.question: Over 300 random builds with 4 versions and 2 sets of flags, how many compiles, hits and stale objects?
questions.explanation: The compiled output contained its whole input so a stale one would be recognised.

questions.question: Why do real tools hash the preprocessed text and not only the source file?
options: The output also depends on every header the file includes, which the source text does not show
questions.explanation: This lesson's key is one file's text and flags, which the docs say it is.
